title: Japan's 'Human Refrigerator' Offers Rapid Cooling as Deadly Heatwaves Intensify
excerpt: A walk-in cooling booth that chills the body in five minutes is already showing up in public spaces and worksites as Japan grapples with record hospitalizations from heat stroke.
body:
• Japanese manufacturer SDRS has developed the Do Hiemon Box, a walk-in cooling booth that chills air to 5°C and can relieve heat exhaustion symptoms in five to ten minutes.
  • The booth costs ¥1.5 million (approximately $9,230), runs on a standard plug, and uses half the energy of a portable air conditioner.
  • Japan experienced an unprecedented five-day streak of "kokushobi" — days exceeding 40°C — this summer, with 453 people hospitalized in Tokyo in a single day.
  • The unit has been donated to public buildings and is being deployed at construction sites, factories, and outdoor events across Japan.

Inside Maebashi City Hall in Japan's Gunma Prefecture, a stainless-steel box the size of a vending machine offers something the city's overheated residents increasingly need: a place to get cold, fast. The Do Hiemon Box, developed by Japanese refrigeration manufacturer SDRS and distributed by industrial supplier Trusco Nakayama, is a single-person cooling booth that its makers call a "human refrigerator."

Step inside, sit on the built-in bench, and close the door. Vents at the top and back direct air cooled to 5°C — roughly the temperature of a kitchen refrigerator — toward your head, neck, shoulders, and back. The booth maintains an interior ambient temperature of 15°C. Users report feeling noticeably cooler within five minutes. The system automatically shuts off after 20 minutes to prevent overcooling.

Built for a Crisis

The timing is deliberate. Japan experienced a record-breaking heatwave this summer, with an unprecedented five consecutive "kokushobi" days — a term meteorologists coined last year for days when temperatures exceed 40°C, meaning "cruel heat day." During the worst of it, 453 people were hospitalized for heatstroke in Tokyo in a single day, the highest number since records began over a decade ago. At least 14 people died across the country.

Over 100,000 people were transported to hospitals for heatstroke in a single season last year, a staggering figure that prompted local governments and corporations to search for aggressive countermeasures. The Do Hiemon Box, which went on sale in April at ¥1.5 million (approximately $9,230) plus tax, is aimed squarely at that problem.

How It Works

The booth stands 2,029 millimeters tall and 931 millimeters wide, weighing 293 kilograms. It runs on wheels, requires no installation, and can be powered by a standard 100-volt electrical outlet. Built from stainless-steel panels with polystyrene insulation, the unit carries an IPX3 weather-resistance rating, making it suitable for both indoor and outdoor deployment.

Three cooling modes let users adjust airflow and temperature, and the design targets areas that play a critical role in regulating body temperature — the head, neck, and shoulders. Trusco Nakayama says the booth provides "full body cooling," unlike the battery-powered fan jackets widely used by outdoor laborers in Japan.

Energy consumption is roughly half that of a typical portable air conditioner, according to the manufacturer — a meaningful distinction given that conventional air conditioning contributes approximately 3% of global greenhouse gas emissions through both energy use and refrigerant leakage.

"Japan experienced an unprecedented five-day streak of "kokushobi" — days exceeding 40°C — this summer, with 453 people hospitalized in Tokyo in a single day."

From Worksites to City Halls

The primary market is commercial: construction sites, factories, warehouses, and outdoor workplaces where heat stroke is a serious occupational hazard. But public applications are expanding. One unit was donated to Maebashi City Hall for free public use during business hours.

"While the number of users was low initially, usage has risen to over 30 people per day recently as the weather has warmed up," said Katsutoshi Yagihara, Deputy Chief of the Policy Coordination Unit in Maebashi City's Future Creation Department.

Residents have embraced it. "The air blows from around the neck area, and the breeze isn't uncomfortably cold," one user named Yuri told Japanese media. "Since cooling the neck and limbs is said to lower body temperature, it felt incredibly cool and refreshing."

A Global Problem, A Local Solution

Japan's approach to extreme heat has drawn international attention because the country faces the challenge ahead of most others. But the problem is global. India's own deadly heatwaves — which killed over 100 people during a single week this summer — have raised similar questions about how to protect outdoor workers and vulnerable populations as temperatures climb.

The Do Hiemon Box won't solve the heat crisis alone. But it represents a growing recognition that as climate change makes extreme heat more frequent and more lethal, the response will require not just policy changes but practical engineering solutions that can be deployed quickly, moved easily, and powered cheaply.
